summaries.example: Imagine you promise yourself to practice an instrument for ten minutes each day. Is this a real promise, or is it only a strong decision? If you later change your mind, did you break a duty, or did you simply choose a new plan? Philosophers use questions like this to explore what we owe to ourselves.
summaries.summary: Many people say we owe things to other people, such as keeping promises. Philosophers ask whether we can also owe things to ourselves. Examples include taking care of our health, protecting our future, learning about ourselves, and standing up for our own dignity. The idea is puzzling. If you owe something to yourself, perhaps you can cancel the duty whenever you want. But a rule that can be canceled at any moment may seem less like a real duty and more like a choice. Philosophers disagree about the answer. Some say there are no true obligations to oneself. Some say such obligations exist but cannot be released, because they are about caring and respect rather than rights or contracts. Others say self-release is possible, though it may need to be informed and voluntary rather than careless or confused. The entry also asks how these ideas affect promises to ourselves, body modification, privacy, self-knowledge, self-respect, and difficult questions about life and death.
key_ideas: Some philosophers think we have duties of self-care, such as looking after our health and future.
Other philosophers focus on self-respect: not treating yourself as worthless or as merely a tool.
A puzzle appears because a person might seem able to cancel an obligation owed to themselves.
Philosophers respond in three main ways: deny duties to oneself, defend duties that cannot be canceled, or allow duties that can be canceled in special ways.
The topic connects to promises, privacy, body changes, self-knowledge, and how we treat our future selves.
summaries.why_it_matters: The question changes how we think about self-care and self-respect. It also helps us understand why a choice can be allowed yet still seem unwise, careless, or disrespectful. Thinking about future selves can encourage us to protect important choices without assuming that every risky or unusual choice is wrong. The topic also shows that moral philosophy is not only about how we treat other people; it can include how we relate to ourselves over time.

important_terms.definition: A rule about what someone must do, or what would be wrong to leave undone.
Something that concerns you, even if it is owed to another person. For example, keeping a promise to a friend may concern your own behavior.
An obligation that is owed to you, as if you were both the person who must act and the person who is owed something.
Treating yourself as a person whose choices, safety, and dignity matter.

questions_to_think_about: Is caring for yourself something you owe yourself, or simply something that is good for you?
Can you really make a promise to yourself?
Should your present self always be free to choose what happens to your future self?
What does it mean to respect yourself?

summaries.example: Suppose an 18-year-old promises herself that she will save money for college. A week later, she learns that her income will rise, so buying a laptop now will not endanger that plan. One philosopher might say the original self-promise was merely a resolution. Another might say it created a genuine but waivable obligation, released by new information rather than by a careless change of mood. A third might say it was an unwaivable duty to protect her future interests. The example illustrates why the possibility of self-release does not settle the debate by itself.
summaries.summary: The entry examines whether moral obligations can be owed to the person who has them. Traditional examples divide into self-care, which promotes one’s interests and survival, and self-respect, which concerns dignity and the proper treatment of oneself. These categories can conflict: an action may protect one’s welfare while seeming degrading, or preserve dignity while imposing serious costs. The deeper issue is the difference between an obligation owed to someone and an obligation merely concerning that person. The paradox of self-release arises because obligations seem binding, while rights held by the person to whom one is obligated can often be waived. If the debtor and creditor are the same person, it may seem that the duty can be canceled at will and therefore was never genuinely binding. Philosophers respond in three broad ways. Skeptics deny that duties to oneself exist, interpreting ordinary language as exaggerated advice or resolve. Defenders of unwaivable duties reject the idea that every duty entails a waivable right, often describing self-duties as non-juridical requirements grounded in humanity, value, or care. Defenders of waivable duties accept self-release but argue that a person remains bound until release occurs, and that release may need to be informed, competent, and autonomous. The framework is applied to self-promises, self-sacrifice, suicide, body modification, self-knowledge, self-respect, and digital privacy. The entry leaves open whether the language of obligation fully captures the moral richness of our relation to ourselves.
key_ideas: The debate depends on distinguishing what is owed to oneself from what merely concerns oneself.
The paradox links obligations, rights, and waivers: if duties imply rights, and rights can be waived, self-directed duties may appear unable to bind.
One response denies that genuine obligations to oneself exist; another separates moral duties from legalistic or rights-based claims.
Some theories use different perspectives within one life, especially the standpoint of a future self, to explain duties not to damage future options.
Self-promises may be genuine promises, useful resolutions, or something in between; the dispute turns partly on whether release can be meaningful.
Applications include self-care, self-respect, privacy, body modification, self-knowledge, suicide, and limits on self-sacrifice.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate clarifies several everyday judgments that otherwise seem inconsistent. We may think people are free to make choices about their bodies while also criticizing reckless decisions that severely restrict their future options. We may praise sacrifice without believing everyone is required to sacrifice themselves. We may regard privacy as a personal interest and also as something people have reason to protect as a matter of self-respect. The theories also have social implications: views about duties to oneself can influence how we understand paternalism, blame, protest, oppression, and the protection of personal information. important_terms.definition: A normative requirement: a reason that normally makes an action necessary and makes failing to perform it wrong, other things equal.
An obligation owed to a particular person, rather than merely an obligation that concerns that person. This distinction is central to the debate.
An obligation concerning oneself, such as maintaining health, without necessarily being owed to oneself in the strict sense.
The apparent problem that an obligation to oneself could be waived by the same person who is bound, making the obligation seem nonbinding.
A view that duties to oneself exist but do not generate rights against oneself or a power to cancel the duty.
A view that a person can release themselves from an obligation, although the release may need to be autonomous, informed, or otherwise valid.
A morally permissible act that is better than another permissible alternative, such as an unusually generous sacrifice.
The authority to make important choices about one’s own body and life, subject to disagreement about its limits.

questions_to_think_about: Does a duty necessarily correspond to someone’s right, or can there be duties without rights?
If you can cancel a self-promise, what makes it more than an intention?
Can a present person wrong a future version of themselves, and how should future interests be weighed against present freedom?
Should self-respect sometimes require accepting fewer opportunities rather than changing oneself to satisfy unfair prejudice?
Are duties to oneself fundamentally different from duties to other people?

summaries.example: Jordan tells himself, “I promise I will stop checking my phone during homework.” Later, he wants to cancel the promise. One view says this was only a resolution, like making a plan. Another says it was a real promise, but Jordan can release himself from it. A third says he has a duty to protect his attention and future goals, even if he would rather quit. Philosophers ask what makes one of these explanations best.
summaries.summary: Moral philosophy often asks what we owe other people. This entry asks whether we can owe something to ourselves. Possible examples include caring for our health, protecting our future choices, learning about our motives, keeping private information safe, and refusing to accept humiliating treatment. Philosophers often separate self-care from self-respect. Self-care aims at one’s welfare, while self-respect concerns dignity and the proper value one gives oneself. These aims can conflict, so there is no simple list of duties that everyone accepts. The central puzzle concerns cancellation. If you owe a friend money, your friend may release you from paying. But if you owe yourself something, it seems that you can release yourself whenever you wish. A duty that is always optional may not be a real duty. One response says there are no genuine duties to oneself; talk about them really means that an action is wise, permitted, or a way of showing resolve. A second response says duties to oneself exist but are not the sort of duties that create rights or can be waived. A third response says self-release can happen, but it may need to be thoughtful and informed, rather than the result of confusion or weakness. The entry applies these ideas to self-promises, future selves, self-sacrifice, body changes, self-knowledge, self-respect, and privacy. It presents these as live disagreements rather than settled answers.
key_ideas: Philosophers distinguish an obligation owed to you from one that merely affects you.
Self-care and self-respect are two major kinds of proposed duties to oneself, and they can point in different directions.
The self-release paradox asks whether a duty can still bind you when you can cancel it yourself.
Some philosophers reject duties to oneself; others defend duties without waivable rights; others accept self-release but place conditions on it.
The debate helps explain self-promises, future choices, privacy, body modification, and whether self-sacrifice is required or optional.
summaries.why_it_matters: People make choices that affect their health, dignity, privacy, and future opportunities. The debate helps us ask whether these choices are merely personal preferences or can also raise moral questions. It also helps explain why freedom does not automatically make every choice wise, and why a choice that is good for others may still not be required if it seriously harms the person making it. Finally, it shows how ideas about the self can affect laws, social expectations, and the way we respond to people facing difficult situations.

important_terms.definition: A moral requirement about what a person must do.
An obligation that concerns you but is owed to someone else, such as a promise to a friend about your own behavior.
A duty that is owed to the same person who must perform it.
A puzzle about how a person can be bound by a duty if that same person can cancel it.
A claim or authority that can sometimes be given up by the person who has it.
A theory saying that duties to oneself cannot be canceled, perhaps because they are about human value rather than contracts.
An action that is allowed and especially good, but not required, such as an unusually brave rescue.

questions_to_think_about: Is a promise to yourself different from a strong decision?
Can a person have a duty that no one has the right to demand?
When should your future interests limit what you do now?
Can protecting your dignity require taking a risk or giving up an advantage?
